% =========================================================== abstract
\begin{abstract}
A learned image decoder spends the same computation on every frame regardless of
what the frame contains. We add an early-exit ladder to the intra decoder of
DCVC-UF~\cite{dcvcuf}, cut each frame into tiles, and let every tile leave the
trunk at whichever of $K$ exits is deep enough for it. The encoder is frozen and
the coded payload is unchanged, so the method deploys against existing
bitstreams. On the full \NumSeq-sequence common test set a $0.1\dB$ budget buys
\MainLowRate\% of the decoder's multiply--accumulates at the lowest rate and
\MainHighRate\% at the highest, for a BD-Rate cost of \BdRateALow\%.

Four findings are worth more than the headline. \textbf{(i)}~A quality budget
only buys compute inside a bounded window: below a \emph{floor} set by tiling no
allocation is feasible, above a \emph{saturation} point every tile already sits
on the cheapest rung, and the working budget uses \BandUseLow\% of that window at
the lowest rate and \BandUseHigh\% at the highest. Both ends are in closed form,
seven structural propositions are verified numerically rather than asserted, and
the window turns out to be almost all of the rate dependence: five rates
\BandRawSpread\ points apart at a matched decibel collapse to
\BandSpreadMean\ once the budget is measured in units of each rate's own band.
\textbf{(ii)}~Tiling is expensive and its cost is governed by depth, not area:
the seam follows a power law in the number of per-tile convolutions with a
fitted exponent near two, where the corrupted-area fraction usually quoted is
wrong by $160$--$264\%$.
\textbf{(iii)}~The exact remedy --- give each convolution its real neighbour ---
is bit-identical at uniform depth and \emph{destroys} the allocation under
routing, because routing is the deliberate violation of the condition that makes
it exact. \textbf{(iv)}~Operations are an \emph{optimistic} bound on this method and the
optimism grows with the saving: \WallSorted\% of wall-clock arrives against a
\WallPredicted\% arithmetic prediction at the lowest rate, \WallHighMeasured\%
against \WallHighPredicted\% at the highest. Sorting the tiles once by exit
depth is bit-identical and recovers a fifth of the shortfall.

Signalling the exit map costs \MapBits\ bits per frame; predicting it at the
decoder costs none and gives up \GapMin--\GapMax\ points. The two are ends of
one scale rather than two designs: overriding the worst fifth of tiles recovers
\HybridRecoverFifthLow--\HybridRecoverFifthHigh\% of that gap for
\HybridBitsFifth\ bits, and at \HybridBeatsAN\ of \HybridBeatsAOf\ rates half
the map \emph{beats} the whole of it, because the hybrid has two multipliers
where the signalled configuration has one. A learned predictor should also be
made to beat a free one: routing on the bits the entropy model has already spent
per tile needs no parameters, no training and no bits, and it beats our
\RouterParams-parameter head to within \RateRankLosesBy\ points at every rate,
and beats it at the \RateRankNWins\ lowest.

We also find that the method is governed by tile count far more than by content
--- three 1080p classes of very different material agree within three points
while a $416{\times}240$ class saves a third as much --- and that an exit map
transfers across frames almost perfectly but not across rates.
\end{abstract}

% =========================================================== introduction
\section{Introduction}

Learned codecs are usually compared on rate and distortion, with complexity
reported as a single number: so many GMAC per frame, so many milliseconds. That
number is a constant. A learned decoder runs the same graph on a page of text and
on a cloudless sky, and the sky is not harder.

Classification networks abandoned this a decade ago. Early-exit
architectures~\cite{branchynet,msdnet,sdn} attach classifiers at intermediate
depths and stop as soon as the prediction is confident, and the literature around
them is mature~\cite{scardapane2020,eesurvey,ztw}. Super-resolution adopted the
same idea spatially: ClassSR~\cite{classsr} routes image patches to networks of
different capacity by difficulty, and APE~\cite{aptnet} exits patches at
different depths of one network. Learned compression has taken a different
route --- slimmable autoencoders~\cite{slimcae,slimvc} give one model several
complexity levels, but the level is chosen \emph{per stream}, not per region, and
switching it changes the bitstream.

We ask the spatial-adaptivity question inside a learned decoder, under a
constraint that makes the answer deployable: \textbf{the encoder is frozen and
the coded payload is unchanged}. Whatever we do must consume the bitstream the
released encoder already produces. That rules out re-training the analysis
transform, changing the entropy model, or altering the latent --- and it leaves
exactly one place to spend adaptivity, the synthesis transform.

Our method, FLEX-UF, is an exit ladder over the twelve residual blocks of the
DCVC-UF intra decoder. The first $j$ blocks run over the whole frame; the rest
run per tile, on a shrinking set of tiles, and that shrinkage is the saving. Each
exit hands its feature to the shared head through a small pointwise adapter,
zero-initialised so that at step zero the deepest exit reproduces the released
decoder bit-exactly.

Making this work turned out to depend less on the ladder than on two things that
have little to do with early exit as usually studied.

\paragraph{Tiling has a price, and it is large.} Spatial adaptivity needs tiles,
and the moment a frame becomes tiles every $3\times3$ convolution at a tile
border reads invented values. On this decoder the resulting error is
\SeamZerosHigh$\dB$ at high rate under the stock padding rule --- several times
the entire budget the method works to, and paid before any tile has saved a
single operation. Section~\ref{sec:seam} treats padding as an \emph{estimator} of
the unseen neighbour and measures four of them; the ordering is not the obvious
one.

\paragraph{A quality budget has a working range.} Because tiling costs something
even when nothing exits early, there is a \emph{floor}: budgets below it admit no
allocation at all. And because the ladder has a shallowest rung, there is a
\emph{saturation} point above which every tile is already there and more quality
buys nothing. Between them the budget genuinely trades quality for compute.
Section~\ref{sec:operating} measures both ends at every rate and shows the
working budget uses \BandUseLow\% of that window at low rate and \BandUseHigh\%
at high rate.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep2pt
\item A tile-adaptive early-exit ladder for a learned image decoder that leaves
      the encoder and the coded payload untouched, saving \MainLowRate\% to
      \MainHighRate\% of decoder MACs for $0.1\dB$ on the full CTC set.
\item The floor/saturation characterisation of a quality budget, with both ends
      measured, and the observation that the architectural ceiling is reachable
      at low rate --- so beyond \SatLow$\dB$ at $q0$ the limit is the ladder, not
      the budget.
\item A quantitative account of the tiling penalty: what it costs, what removes
      it for free, why a higher-order border estimator is worse than a
      zeroth-order one, and why a learned repair module is not worth its
      compute even with a perfect gate.
\item Two allocation regimes --- an encoder-side search that signals a
      $\sim$\MapBits-bit map per frame, and a decoder-side predictor that signals
      nothing --- with the bits and the compute charged on both sides, and the
      continuum between them: overriding the worst fifth of tiles recovers
      \HybridRecoverFifthLow--\HybridRecoverFifthHigh\% of the gap, and at
      \HybridBeatsAN\ of \HybridBeatsAOf\ rates half the map beats all of it,
      because the hybrid has two multipliers where the signalled configuration
      has one.
\item A parameter-free control that a learned router has to beat and usually is
      not measured against. Routing on the bits the entropy model already spent
      per tile costs nothing, adds nothing to the stream, and beats our trained
      head to within \RateRankLosesBy\ points at every rate and beats it at the
      \RateRankNWins\ lowest --- while agreeing with the oracle on fewer tiles
      than the head does.
\item A wall-clock result: operations over-predict the saving by about a fifth,
      and a bit-identical reordering of the per-tile loop recovers a fifth of
      that --- \WallSorted\% realised against a \WallPredicted\% prediction.
\end{enumerate}

% =========================================================== related work
\section{Related work}

\paragraph{Early exit.} BranchyNet~\cite{branchynet} and MSDNet~\cite{msdnet}
established the pattern of intermediate classifiers with a confidence rule;
SDN~\cite{sdn} framed it as mitigating overthinking, and ZTW~\cite{ztw} recycles
earlier predictions. Training all exits jointly follows
Scardapane~\etal~\cite{scardapane2020}; distillation between exits follows
Phuong and Lampert~\cite{phuong2019}, with the caveat from~\cite{msd2024} that
too large a student--teacher gap hurts the shallowest exits --- which is why our
distillation is between \emph{adjacent} exits. All of this work exits on a
confidence signal computed from the network's own output. A decoder has no such
signal: there is no class posterior, and the quantity that would decide is the
error against a source the decoder cannot see (Section~\ref{sec:alloc}).

\paragraph{Spatially adaptive inference.} ClassSR~\cite{classsr} sorts
super-resolution patches into easy/medium/hard and runs a different network on
each; APE~\cite{aptnet} exits patches at different depths; Glance-and-Focus
~\cite{glancefocus} spends resolution adaptively. These share our per-region
premise, and share the tiling problem, though the cost of tile borders is rarely
quantified. To our knowledge the estimator view of border padding and its
measured ordering (Section~\ref{sec:seam}) is new; the closest prior work is the
per-channel AR(1) padding of Kaseva~\etal~\cite{arls}, which we implement and
evaluate.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/positioning}}
\caption{\textbf{Where this sits.} Complexity control in learned compression
varies the model; we vary how much of a fixed model runs where. The last column
is what makes the difference operational: every other row requires a decoder that
matches the encoder that produced the stream.}
\label{tab:positioning}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Complexity control in learned compression.} SlimCAE~\cite{slimcae}
and slimmable video codecs~\cite{slimvc} expose several widths of one model.
The choice is per stream and it changes the encoder, so the bitstream is not
interchangeable. DCVC-FM~\cite{dcvcfm} and DCVC-UF~\cite{dcvcuf} reduce cost
architecturally, for every frame equally. Rate--distortion--complexity has since
become an explicit third axis: Gao~\etal~\cite{gao2024rdc} tune spatial context
usage to trade decode cost against rate, Ho~\etal~\cite{ho2024rdctradeoffs}
survey where conditional residual coding sits on that surface, and
Zhang and Gao~\cite{zhang2025raterouting} route \emph{whole frames} to one of
several jointly-trained coding paths, spending less computation on cheaper
frames. All of these vary the model, and all of them change what the encoder
emits. Our axis is orthogonal: the model is fixed, the bitstream is fixed, and
only \emph{how much of the decoder runs where} varies.

\paragraph{The closest neighbour.} Blard~\etal~\cite{spatialcompetition} also
partition an image into regions, also choose per region by a rate--distortion
cost computed at the encoder, and also transmit a mode map --- the skeleton of
our configuration A. Two things differ. Their regions choose among several
\emph{separately trained} codecs, so the decoder must hold all of them and its
complexity is that of one codec regardless of the choice; the map buys rate, not
compute. Ours choose a prefix length of a single trunk, so the weights are shared
by construction and the map buys compute at fixed rate. And because their
alternatives are unrelated networks, no decoder-side predictor could stand in for
the encoder's search, whereas the nesting that makes our exits prefixes of one
another is exactly what makes configuration B possible at all.

\paragraph{Signalling versus prediction.} That a decoder is \emph{told} a mode
decision rather than inferring it is the norm in standardised video coding: HEVC
\cite{hevc} and VVC~\cite{vvc} transmit partitioning, prediction mode and
transform tree. We evaluate both and treat the signalled variant as the
conventional design.

\paragraph{Deferring to an oracle under a budget.} Configuration~C, where a
predictor decides most cases and a small budget of the hardest ones is handed to
something exact, is the shape of selective prediction~\cite{geifman2017selective}
and learning to defer~\cite{madras2018l2d,mozannar2020consistent}, and of the
budgeted variant of the latter~\cite{desalvo2025budgeted}. Two things differ and
both make our case easier. The expert here is the encoder's own search, so it is
exact, always available, and costs nothing at test time --- what is scarce is not
the expert's attention but the \emph{bits} needed to say what it decided. And the
selection rule is not learned: because the objective is separable over tiles, the
optimal set of size $s$ at a fixed multiplier is exactly the $s$ largest regrets,
which the encoder can compute. The open question in that literature --- who to
defer, and how to learn it --- has a closed form here, and what remains is the
question we measure, which is how concentrated the regret is.

\paragraph{Allocating a budget over units.} The construction we use is not new
and should not be presented as such. Shoham and Gersho~\cite{shoham1988} showed
that for a finite set of per-unit operating points, a Lagrangian sweep decouples
the allocation across units and traces exactly the lower convex hull of the
achievable set; Ortega and Ramchandran~\cite{ortega1998} made it standard
practice in image and video coding. What we add is the structure this particular
operating set has: a floor below which no allocation is feasible, a saturation
point above which none improves, and a measurement of what the convex-hull
restriction costs (Section~\ref{sec:operating}). The same relaxation has
resurfaced for test-time compute in language models~\cite{ctca}, with per-instance
decoupling and a binary search on the multiplier --- the identical structure in a
domain with no rate axis, which we read as evidence that the floor/saturation
characterisation is worth stating generally.

\paragraph{How much is there to gain?} Bounding what adaptive inference could
achieve is itself a line of work. Hasan~\etal~\cite{adaptivelimits} derive an
oracle bound on efficiency at fixed accuracy, given per-model resource and
accuracy, and report $43$--$121\times$ on ImageNet and $7$--$81\times$ on
HellaSwag. Their bound has a ceiling and no floor, because the largest model in
their family attains the reference accuracy by definition. Spatial adaptivity
introduces one: cutting a frame into tiles costs quality even when every tile
runs to full depth, so the reference is unreachable at \emph{any} compute and
the feasible set of budgets is an interval rather than a ray. That interval, and
both of its ends, is what Section~\ref{sec:operating} characterises.

\paragraph{Tile boundaries.} Every method that processes an image in
independently-computed tiles meets the same artefact, and the remedies in the
literature are overlap and averaging, local padding from neighbouring
patches~\cite{localpadding}, training with overlaps~\cite{overlaptrain}, and
fitted extrapolation~\cite{arls}. Local padding is the closest to the exact
remedy we describe in Section~\ref{sec:coupling}, and the difference is
accounting: it pads every convolutional layer and does not report the cost, while
we pad only the $0.29\%$ of each block that has any spatial extent, which is what
makes the exact fix cost $0.032\%$ of the decode rather than a multiplier on all
of it. To our knowledge the estimator view of the padding rule, the measured
ordering of four estimators, and the dependence of the penalty on per-tile depth
(Section~\ref{sec:seam}) have not been reported.

\paragraph{Where the time goes.} DCVC-RT~\cite{dcvcrt} argues that operational
rather than computational complexity is the speed bottleneck for neural codecs,
evidenced by channel reductions that yield linear rather than quadratic speedups.
Section~\ref{sec:wallclock} is an instance of that claim inside one loop:
\WallPredicted\% of operations removed buys \WallSorted\% of time, and
\WallSortedGain\ points of the difference come back from reordering the loop with
the arithmetic untouched.

% =========================================================== method
\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/sys_pipeline.png}
\caption{\textbf{FLEX-UF end to end.} Grey is frozen and never touched; blue is
inherited from DCVC-UF and fine-tuned; orange and green are new. The first $j$
block groups run over the whole frame, the rest run per tile on a shrinking
active set, and the exit map that drives the shrinkage comes either from an
encoder-side search (A) or from a decoder-side predictor (B).}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Where the computation is}

The DCVC-UF intra decoder is one upsampling block, twelve \texttt{DepthConvBlock}s
and a head, costing $453.5$ GMAC per 1080p frame. The twelve blocks are $89.4\%$
of it, which is why the ladder is built across them. Inside one block at
$C{=}384$ channels, the only operator with any spatial extent is a $3\times3$
depthwise convolution costing $9C$ against the block's $8C^2 + 9C$ ---
$\mathbf{0.29\%}$. That single number recurs throughout this paper: it is why
tile borders damage the picture, why our adapters are pointwise on purpose, and
why the exact remedy of Section~\ref{sec:coupling} is affordable.

\subsection{The exit ladder}

With $K$ exits over the twelve blocks and split depth $j$, groups
$0,\dots,j-1$ run full frame for every tile and groups $j,\dots,K-1$ run per
tile. A tile assigned exit $k$ runs groups $j..k$ and then leaves. Writing $c_k$
for the cost of exit $k$ in units of one released decode, the cost of a frame
with exit map $\mathbf{k}$ is $\frac{1}{T}\sum_t c_{k_t}$ over its $T$ tiles.

Two consequences are easy to state wrongly. Exits shallower than $j$ are
indistinguishable --- the first $j$ groups run for every tile regardless --- so
the usable ladder has $K-j$ distinct costs, and the \emph{architectural ceiling}
is
\begin{equation}
S_{\max} = 100\,(1 - c_j)\;\%,
\label{eq:ceiling}
\end{equation}
attained when every tile takes exit $j$. For our shipped setting ($K{=}6$,
$j{=}2$, $256$\,px tiles) $S_{\max} = \Ceiling\%$. We show in
Section~\ref{sec:operating} that this bound is \emph{reached} in practice at low
rate, which makes it an operating point rather than an asymptote.

\subsection{Exit adapters}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/adapters.png}
\caption{\textbf{Inside an exit adapter.} Both kinds are entirely pointwise, so
no adapter adds receptive field and none of them contributes any tile-boundary
penalty. Capacity is matched to the number of blocks the exit skips, and charged
for: an exit-2 tile saves six blocks minus $0.25$, not six.}
\label{fig:adapters}
\end{figure}

An early exit hands the shared head a feature the head was not fitted to. The
adapter is the correction. We use a residual $1\times1$,
$\mathrm{Ad}(f) = f + Wf$ with $W$ zero-initialised, for exits that skip little,
and the pointwise expand/activate/contract pair of the block's own FFN for exits
that skip four blocks or more (Fig.~\ref{fig:adapters}). Both are
\emph{pointwise by design}: a $3\times3$ inside an adapter would add seam damage
precisely at the tiles that took an early exit, the ones least able to afford it.
Zero-initialising the last layer makes every adapter exactly the identity at step
zero, so the deepest exit is bit-exactly the released decoder before training
begins and every shallow exit starts from ``the decoder as it is''.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/adapter_gain.png}
\caption{\textbf{What the adapters are worth.} \textbf{a}, each exit with and
without its adapter. \textbf{b}, the dB the adapter recovers. \textbf{c}, the
same against the number of blocks the exit skips --- the design rationale,
measured.}
\label{fig:adaptergain}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/adapters_ablation}}
\caption{\textbf{What the adapters are worth.} dB below the release with every
tile at that exit, with the trained adapters and with each set back to the
identity it was initialised to. $^{\dagger}$ the deepest exit has no adapter by
construction and is the control.}
\label{tab:adapters}
\end{table}

Zeroing them measures what they learned, since the identity is exactly what they
were initialised to (Table~\ref{tab:adapters}). Without adapters the shallowest
exit costs \AdapterNoneHigh$\dB$ at $q63$ --- forty-four times the budget --- and
the adapter buys \AdapterGainHigh$\dB$ back. The gain grows with rate and with
the number of blocks the exit skips, which is the design rationale measured
rather than argued, and the deepest exit moves by exactly zero. The adapters are
not a refinement of the ladder; without them it has no usable rung.

\subsection{Allocation}
\label{sec:alloc}

Given per-tile distortions $D_{t,k}$ and costs $c_k$, the allocation that
minimises distortion at a compute budget is the Lagrangian
\begin{equation}
k^{*}_t(\lambda) \;=\; \arg\min_k \; \bigl[\, D_{t,k} + \lambda\, c_k \,\bigr],
\label{eq:lagrangian}
\end{equation}
with $\lambda$ found by bisection so the frame lands on the quality budget.
Both quantities in~(\ref{eq:lagrangian}) are available \emph{to the encoder},
which holds the source. This gives configuration~\textbf{A}: the encoder searches
and transmits the map, which entropy-codes to $\sim$\MapBits\ bits per 1080p
frame, or \MapOverheadLow\% of a typical bitrate, and costs the decoder nothing.

What it costs the \emph{encoder} depends on how the table is built, and the
difference is larger than it looks. Measured at 1080p against one tiled decode as
the unit: the deployed table, $K$ tiled decodes, is $4.6\times$; the full-frame
table of Section~\ref{sec:method} is $1.4\times$. The full-frame table is the one
Section~5 shows must not be used to \emph{report} quality --- but it can be used
to \emph{rank}. Using it for the argmin and the deployed path only to check the
budget, the two searches agree on $85\%$ of tiles and land within $0.4$ points of
saving of each other ($19.0\%$ against $18.6\%$, both under budget). So the exact
search costs $4.6$ decodes and a practical encoder need not pay it.

The decoder cannot evaluate~(\ref{eq:lagrangian}): $D_{t,k}$ is the error against
a source it never sees. This is not a hard estimation problem, it is a missing
variable, and no architecture removes it. Configuration~\textbf{B} therefore
\emph{predicts}: a $144$K-parameter head reads the full-frame stem feature, the
decoded latent $\hat{y}$, the entropy model's scales and the quality index, emits
logits $z_t$, and decides
\begin{equation}
\hat{k}_t \;=\; \arg\max_k \;\bigl[\, \log \mathrm{softmax}(z_t)_k
                                       - \beta\, c_k \,\bigr],
\label{eq:router}
\end{equation}
with $\beta$ bisected exactly as $\lambda$ is. Nothing is added to the file. The
head is trained against a \emph{frozen} decoder with a cost-sensitive
cross-entropy to the oracle's choice, each tile weighted by the regret of
choosing wrongly, plus loss-free load balancing~\cite{lossfreebalance} biased
toward the oracle's own exit distribution rather than toward uniform --- at a
high $\lambda$ the oracle genuinely does send every tile to one exit, and forcing
spread there would force mistakes.

\subsection{Training}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/training_scheme.png}
\caption{\textbf{Training.} One forward pass produces all $K$ reconstructions, so
the ladder is trained as one object rather than as $K$ models. The encoder side
--- $61.5\%$ of the parameters --- is frozen, which is what makes the released
decoder and ours comparable on the \emph{same} latent.}
\label{fig:training}
\end{figure*}

All exits are decoded every step and the objective is
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L} \;=\; \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RD}}
   \;+\; w_a\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}}
   \;+\; w_d\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{distill}},
\end{equation}
with
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RD}} = \lambda \sum_k \alpha_k \mathrm{MSE}_k / \sum_k \alpha_k + \mathrm{bpp}$
the released rate--distortion loss averaged over exits;
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anchor}} = \lambda\lVert \hat{x}_{K-1} - \hat{x}^{\mathrm{rel}}\rVert^2$
pinning the deepest exit to the released decoder, so the reference every saving
is quoted against cannot drift away underneath the measurement; and
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{distill}} = \frac{1}{K-1}\sum_k \lVert f_k - \mathrm{sg}(f_{k+1})\rVert^2 / \mathrm{Var}(f_{k+1})$
supervising adapters in feature space, exit $k$ imitating exit $k{+}1$. Feature
space rather than pixels because the head is a fixed map from feature to RGB and
matching the deeper feature is the stronger constraint --- $384$ dense channels of
target instead of $3$; adjacent rather than deepest for the reason
in~\cite{msd2024}.

Critically, the adapters are trained \emph{through the tiled decode path they are
deployed in}. Training them full-frame and tiling only at inference loses
$0.14$--$0.24\dB$; training through the deployed path gains $0.51$--$0.90\dB$.
The sign of the effect flips.

% =========================================================== the seam
\section{The price of tiles}
\label{sec:seam}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/seam_problem.png}
\caption{\textbf{The artefact, before anything is done about it.} One frame
decoded twice from the \emph{same} bitstream with the same weights, every tile at
full depth, stock zero padding --- no early exit anywhere. The only difference is that the right-hand
decode was tiled. The error map is the tile lattice and nothing else.}
\label{fig:seamproblem}
\end{figure}

A $3\times3$ depthwise at feature position $(i,j)$ computes
$\sum_{u,v} w_{u,v}\, f_{i+u,\,j+v}$. Decoded full frame those neighbours exist;
decoded per tile they do not, and the kernel is handed whatever the padding rule
invents. Each convolution extends the contaminated region by one ring, so with $b$
per-tile blocks on a tile of side $F$ the fraction of the tile within reach of an
invented value is $1 - ((F-2b)/F)^2$, which is $0.750$ at our shipped $F{=}32$,
$b{=}8$: not a thin border but a structured error across most of the tile
(Fig.~\ref{fig:seamproblem}).

That fraction says which pixels are affected, not how badly, and it is not what
governs the penalty. Sweeping the split depth --- which sweeps $b$ from 12 to 0,
with $b{=}0$ as an exact zero-seam control --- gives
\begin{equation}
\text{seam} \;\propto\; b^{\alpha}, \qquad \alpha \approx 2,
\label{eq:contam}
\end{equation}
$\alpha = 2.38$ at $q0$ falling to $1.93$ at $q63$, $r = 0.98$--$0.995$ in
log--log. Fitted with one free scale the area fraction is wrong by $160$--$264\%$
where the power law is wrong by $12$--$22\%$. Fixing the exponent at exactly two
costs a factor of two, $31$--$38\%$ --- the square is the right shape and not
quite the right law. The exponent has a reading: the
count of contaminated pixels grows like perimeter times depth, $\propto b$, and
the error accumulated in each grows with how many convolutions reached it, again
$\propto b$. The area law saturates once every pixel is touched; the penalty does
not, and that is where it fails.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/contamination.png}
\caption{\textbf{The seam against per-tile depth.} Sweeping the split depth
sweeps $b$; $b{=}0$ is an exact control and measures $0.0000\dB$ at all three
rates. \textbf{a}, the measurement with the fitted power law. \textbf{b},
both models against $q63$ with one free scale each. \textbf{c}, mean relative
error. The area fraction saturates once every pixel is contaminated; the penalty
does not.}
\label{fig:contam}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Padding is an estimator}

The useful way to see border padding is as an \emph{estimator} of the unseen
neighbour, whose error is the seam. Table~\ref{tab:padding} measures four, with
early exit switched off so tiling is the only difference from a full-frame
decode.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/padding}
\caption{\textbf{Border estimators}, dB below the released decoder on the same
latent, $256$\,px tiles, full CTC. Lower is better. The zeroth-order hold beats
the first-order extrapolation by a wide margin, and the fitted AR(1) wins on
quality while costing $+10.7\%$ of decode wall-clock.}
\label{tab:padding}
\end{table}

Two results deserve emphasis. \textbf{A higher-order estimator is worse.}
Extrapolating the local gradient past a boundary amplifies whatever noise sits on
that boundary; assuming local constancy does not. Guessing harder is not the same
as guessing better, and the gap is not small: \SeamLinearHigh$\dB$ against
\SeamReplHigh$\dB$ at $q63$. \textbf{The best estimator loses on cost.} The
per-channel AR(1) fit of~\cite{arls} reaches \SeamArlsHigh$\dB$, an improvement of
about $0.02\dB$ over replication, for $10.7\%$ of decode wall-clock. Against a
$0.1\dB$ budget and a $\sim$30\% saving that trade does not close, and we drop it.

\subsection{What actually removes the seam}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/seam_vs_qp.png}
\caption{\textbf{The tiling penalty across the whole rate range}, every tile at
full depth. The two steps that matter cost nothing, and the largest single
factor is training the ladder with the seam present. Panel (b): the floor is
charged \emph{inside} the quality budget and consumes a growing share of it.}
\label{fig:seamqp}
\end{figure}

Tile size is free --- a tiled decode's MAC count does not depend on it at all ---
and the damage scales with the tile perimeter (Table~\ref{tab:tilesize}). What it
costs instead is routing granularity: 40 tiles per 1080p frame at $256$\,px
against 160 at $128$\,px.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/tilesize}
\caption{\textbf{Tile size}, dB at $q63$. Doubling the side roughly halves the
penalty, as~(\ref{eq:contam}) predicts, and costs no computation.}
\label{tab:tilesize}
\end{table}

The largest factor of all is the one easiest to overlook. Replicate padding
leaves \SeamReplHigh$\dB$ at $q63$ on the untrained ladder; after training the
same configuration leaves \FloorHigh$\dB$. More than two thirds of what the
estimator could not fix is absorbed by weights learning to live with it
(Fig.~\ref{fig:seamqp}). No module in this paper removes as much.

\subsection{A learned repair module, and why we reject it}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/seam_module.png}
\caption{\textbf{Grid seam repair.} A correction gated by position within a tile,
applied once to the stitched frame. The trained gate learns the boundary ring
(0.76) but never switches off inside (0.145 over 94\% of pixels), and the
measured effect follows: it helps on the ring and hurts everywhere else.}
\label{fig:seammodule}
\end{figure}

Since the tile lattice is known exactly at training and inference, a repair can
be \emph{told} where to look rather than having to infer it:
$\mathrm{Rep}(f) = f + G[i \bmod P,\, j \bmod P]\cdot
\mathrm{PW}(\mathrm{WSiLU}(\mathrm{DW}_{3\times3}(f)))$, with $G$ a $P{\times}P$
gate shared over channels and initialised at $\exp(-d/\tau)$. It costs $0.95\%$
of the decode.

It does not earn that. Splitting per-pixel error by distance from the nearest
tile boundary, the module gains $0.27\%$ in the $0$--$4$\,px band ($6.2\%$ of
pixels) and loses $0.04$--$0.05\%$ everywhere else. Even with a \emph{perfect}
gate --- zero correction in the interior, the boundary gain unchanged --- the
ceiling on what it could earn is
\begin{equation*}
0.062 \times 0.000047 \times 0.0027 \,/\, 4.30\!\times\!10^{-5}
\;\approx\; 0.0008\dB,
\end{equation*}
for $0.95\%$ of the decode. We rejected AR(1) padding at $0.0019\dB$ per point of
decode; this is worse by an order of magnitude. Tightening the gate cannot rescue
it, because there is almost nothing left to win.

\subsection{Removing the cause, and why it does not help}
\label{sec:coupling}

Because only $0.29\%$ of each block has spatial extent, the exact fix is
affordable: give the $3\times3$ its real neighbour from a shared canvas, for
$+0.032\%$ of the decode --- thirty times less than the repair module. And it is
exact. At uniform depth a coupled tiled decode is bit-identical to a full-frame
one, once the comparison is not confounded by the repair module, which runs on the
stitched canvas and has no full-frame counterpart:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\toprule
at uniform depth & $\max|\text{tiled}-\text{full}|$ \\
\midrule
coupling, repair on (as shipped) & $1.13\times10^{-2}$ \\
coupling, repair off & $\mathbf{0}$ \\
replicate padding, repair off & $6.06\times10^{-2}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

It also removes most of the floor: switched on at inference, the floor falls from
$0.036$ to $0.003\dB$ at $q0$ and from $0.056$ to $0.030$ at $q63$, i.e.\ \CoupFloorDropLow\%
and \CoupFloorDropHigh\% of the tiling penalty.

\textbf{And it destroys the allocation.} At the same $0.1\dB$ budget the saving
falls from \CoupPaddedMid\% to \CoupCoupledMid\% at $q32$ and from
\CoupPaddedHigh\% to \CoupCoupledHigh\% at $q63$.

The reason is structural rather than incidental, and it is the condition in the
exactness statement. Coupling is exact when every tile is at the \emph{same}
depth --- and routing is the deliberate violation of that condition. With
replicate padding a tile is entirely independent of its neighbours, so the
allocation is free to give adjacent tiles any depths it likes. Coupling makes a
tile depend on its neighbours' features, and under routing those neighbours ran a
different number of blocks; a shallow tile reading a deep neighbour's activation
is a configuration the weights have never seen, and that mismatch costs far more
than the seam it removed.

We report this because the natural reading of the exactness result --- that the
exact fix should simply be adopted --- is the wrong one, and because the tension
between coupling and routing is a property of the combination that any
spatially-adaptive decoder will inherit. The caveat that keeps it from being
final is the same one that applies to the repair module: this model was trained
with padding, and a run trained \emph{with} coupling could reverse the result.
The burden is on that run.

% =========================================================== experiments
\section{Experiments}

\paragraph{Setup.} The decoder is fine-tuned on OpenImages~\cite{openimages}
$512{\times}512$ crops with the encoder frozen ($\max|\Delta| = 0$ asserted every
run), one $\lambda$ drawn per sample from a log-spaced range covering all 64
quality indices, so a single set of weights serves the whole rate range.
Evaluation is on the \NumSeq\ sequences of the common test set --- UVG~\cite{uvg},
MCL-JCV~\cite{mcljcv} and HEVC classes B, C, D and E --- one intra frame each.

\paragraph{Measurement protocol.} Two details of the protocol change the numbers
enough to be worth stating. First, the per-tile distortion table
$D_{t,k}$ must be built on the \emph{deployed} decode path --- one tiled decode
per exit --- and not by tapping the exits of a single full-frame forward pass.
The latter is the natural implementation and is correct for training, but with a
full-frame reference on the other side of the ratio the tiling penalty cancels
and the reported quality is that of a decoder nobody ships. On our model the
difference is $+0.035\dB$ at the deepest exit and $+0.008\dB$ at the shallowest;
it is not a constant offset, it grows with how many blocks ran per tile, so it
cannot be corrected after the fact. Second, after the allocation is chosen we
decode that \emph{mixed} map once and report the distortion it actually
produces.

\paragraph{Reporting conventions.} Every dB is measured against the
\emph{released} decoder's full-frame decode of the \emph{same} latent, and our
side is the deployed tiled decode, so the tiling penalty is inside every number.
Savings are fractions of the released decoder's cost; our own deepest exit costs
$1.0095$ of it, and using that as the denominator would flatter every result by
$0.6$--$0.8$ points.

\subsection{Main result}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/qualitative.png}
\caption{\textbf{What the saving looks like.} The same bitstream decoded by the
released decoder and by ours at the $0.1\dB$ operating point, $30.5\%$ fewer
multiply--accumulates. The crop is the tile that gave up the most quality, chosen
automatically, so this is the method's worst case on this frame rather than a
flattering one.}
\label{fig:qual}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/main_results}
\caption{\textbf{Decoder MACs saved} (\%) against the released decoder, per
quality index and quality budget, configuration A. The $0.3$ and $0.5\dB$ rows
sit on the architectural ceiling of Eq.~(\ref{eq:ceiling}) almost everywhere:
past that point a looser budget buys nothing.}
\label{tab:main}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:main} is the headline. At $0.1\dB$ the method saves
\MainLowRate\% at the lowest rate and \MainHighRate\% at the highest, averaging
\MainMean\%. The fall with rate is not an artefact of the ladder: high-rate
reconstructions carry detail the shallow exits cannot reproduce, the floor rises
with rate (Fig.~\ref{fig:seamqp}b), and both push the same way.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/rd_spread.png}
\caption{\textbf{The plane a codec is read on, and the spread behind the mean.}
\textbf{a}, operating points against the released curve. \textbf{b}, the same
with the quality axis expanded; labels are compute saved. \textbf{c}, per
sequence at a matched point near $0.1\dB$; one dot per sequence, bar is the
median.}
\label{fig:rd}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:rd}c is the distribution the headline averages over, and it is
wide. At $q0$ the median sequence saves $38.6\%$ with an interquartile range of
$32.0$--$41.5$, while the worst saves $-1.0\%$ --- the low-resolution sequences of
Section~\ref{sec:resolution}, where two tiles leave nothing to allocate. Reporting
the mean alone would hide both ends.

\subsection{Is per-tile adaptivity necessary?}
\label{sec:necessary}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/exit_map.png}
\caption{\textbf{Where the decoder spends.} Bosphorus at $q32$, a
$0.1\dB$ budget. (a) the assignment overlaid on the frame, (b) the exit index
per tile, (c) the quality each tile gives up, against its \emph{own} full-depth
reference. Water and sky leave at the shallowest rung; the boat and the
shoreline run deep.}
\label{fig:exitmap}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/static}}
\caption{\textbf{Adaptivity against two controls} at the $0.1\dB$ budget.
$^{\dagger}$ marks uniform depths whose distortion exceeds the budget, so they
are not admissible allocations at all. ``Random'' draws each frame's map from the
oracle's own exit histogram and shuffles it across tiles: same average cost, same
mix of depths, none of the content dependence.}
\label{tab:static}
\end{table}

The obvious alternative to routing tiles is not to route them: run every tile at
the same shallower exit and accept the loss. Table~\ref{tab:static} puts that
option, and two stronger controls, at matched compute.

The uniform rows answer it directly, and the answer sharpens with rate. At the
lowest rate a static decoder can reach exit 3 within the budget and save
$27.0\%$, against the oracle's \MainLowRate\%. At $q48$ and $q63$ the only
uniform depth that fits is the deepest one, which \emph{costs} $0.95\%$ rather
than saving anything --- so there the choice is not between $17\%$ and something
smaller, it is between $17\%$ and nothing. Averaged over rates the best static
allocation saves \BestStaticMean\% where the adaptive one saves \MainMean\%.

The two shuffled rows separate effects that are easy to conflate. Given the
oracle's own exit histogram --- the same mix of depths, hence the same average
cost --- but assigned to tiles at random, quality collapses: what the allocation
buys is not that some tiles run shallower, it is knowing \emph{which} ones can.
The rate-ranked row keeps that histogram and orders it by a signal the decoder
already holds: the bits the entropy model spent on each tile. It is the cheapest
conceivable router --- no parameters, no training, and the number is available
before the trunk starts --- and it is the natural analogue of the confidence
rules used by early-exit classifiers~\cite{branchynet,msdnet}, which likewise
read a signal off the network's own output.

It recovers most of the gap. At $q63$, random costs \RandomDb$\dB$ and the
oracle $0.100\dB$ at identical compute; rate-ranking costs \RateRankDb$\dB$,
i.e.\ \RateRankRecovers\% of
the oracle's advantage over chance, at $0.68$--$0.79$ agreement with the oracle's
map. A learned router therefore has to beat a free baseline that is already three
quarters of the way there --- a comparison we would not have made without this
control, and one we suggest any adaptive-inference paper should report. Given
the oracle's histogram this is a measurement of \emph{ranking} and nothing else;
Section~\ref{sec:raterank} removes that crutch and turns the same signal into a
complete routing rule, which matches the trained head across the whole rate
range. Fig.~\ref{fig:exitmap} shows the assignment the oracle
arrives at.

\subsection{Resolution, and the granularity of a tile}
\label{sec:resolution}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/perclass}
\caption{\textbf{Saving by test class} (\%), at a matched operating point near
$0.1\dB$. ``Tiles'' is how many $256$\,px tiles a frame of that resolution
contains. The method is a function of tile count far more than of content.}
\label{tab:perclass}
\end{table}

Completing the test set exposed a dependence the 1080p-only subset had hidden.
Table~\ref{tab:perclass} groups the saving by class. At 1080p, where a frame is
40 tiles, the method saves $36$--$39\%$ at the lowest rate. At $832{\times}480$
it is 8 tiles and $23.6\%$; at $416{\times}240$ it is 2 tiles and $16.5\%$. At
high rate the small resolutions collapse to \SmallResHigh\% against
\BigResHigh\% for 1080p.

The natural explanation is granularity: with two tiles per frame there is almost
no allocation to make and the Lagrangian degenerates towards a uniform choice.
The natural fix follows --- a tile size chosen relative to the frame, since the
MAC count does not depend on tile size at all and only the seam does.

\textbf{We tested that fix and it mostly does not work.} Comparing the $256$\,px
configuration against a $128$\,px one at $q0$, which multiplies the tile count by
$3.4$:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
class & 256\,px & 128\,px & $\Delta$ \\
\midrule
MCL-JCV (1080p) & 36.3 & 34.3 & $-2.0$ \\
HEVC B (1080p) & 33.8 & 32.1 & $-1.7$ \\
HEVC C ($832{\times}480$) & 20.9 & 17.6 & $-3.3$ \\
HEVC D ($416{\times}240$) & 11.3 & \textbf{13.7} & $\mathbf{+2.4}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Smaller tiles help only at the smallest resolution, where the count goes from two
to eight, and cost between $1.7$ and $3.3$ points everywhere else --- including
at $832{\times}480$, where the count rises from $8$ to $28$ and the saving still
falls. Beyond a modest number of tiles the extra seam buys more than the extra
granularity is worth. The comparison confounds tile size with training, since the
two are different runs, so we report it as indicative; but the direction is
consistent and it is enough to say that a resolution-adaptive tile size is not
the easy win the granularity argument suggests.

\subsection{The working range of a quality budget}
\label{sec:operating}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/saturation_RECIPE512.png}
\caption{\textbf{Three regions, and only the middle one is a design choice.}
Below the floor no allocation meets the budget; above saturation every tile is
already on the cheapest rung. The working $0.1\dB$ budget uses \BandUseLow\% of
the window at the lowest rate and \BandUseHigh\% at the highest.}
\label{fig:operating}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/operating}}
\caption{\textbf{Floor and saturation}, dB below the released decoder. The floor
is what tiling costs with no early exit at all; saturation is where every tile
reaches exit $j$ and the ceiling of Eq.~(\ref{eq:ceiling}) is attained.}
\label{tab:operating}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/theory.png}
\caption{\textbf{The structure of the allocation}, on one frame. \textbf{a},
compute and distortion are monotone in the multiplier. \textbf{b}, the frontier
between the floor (green) and saturation (orange); shaded regions are infeasible
and wasted. \textbf{c}, what the Lagrangian reaches against the exact Pareto set,
enumerated by dynamic programming --- the two curves are indistinguishable.}
\label{fig:theory}
\end{figure}

The construction has enough structure to state as propositions, and we verify
each numerically rather than asserting it (\texttt{scripts/verify\_theory.py},
seven of seven). The allocation decouples per tile; compute is non-increasing and
distortion non-decreasing in $\lambda$; the sweep traces the lower convex hull
and therefore cannot reach an interior point of the achievable set;
$\lambda{=}0$ attains the least distortion the ladder can produce; beyond a
finite $\lambda$, computable in closed form as
$\max_t \max_k (D_{t,j}-D_{t,k})/(c_k-c_j)$, the allocation is the constant map
to exit $j$ at cost exactly $c_j$; and the ceiling is a function of the split
depth alone.

The third of those is the one with a practical edge. Because the sweep reaches
only hull vertices, a budget falling between two of them is not attainable. We
measured what that costs by enumerating the \emph{exact} Pareto set with dynamic
programming over tiles --- feasible because the cost alphabet has four symbols
--- and comparing: the sweep reaches 95 allocations against a Pareto set of 635,
and the loss from convexity is at most $0.05$ saving points
(Fig.~\ref{fig:theory}c). The standard construction is essentially optimal here.

It is worth saying \emph{why} that loss is small, because the reason is
structural and says what would make it smaller. The reachable costs form a
lattice whose spacing is set by how much the mean cost moves when the multiplier
crosses a switching point: $m$ tiles each move one rung, so the spacing is at
most $m\max_k(c_{k+1}-c_k)/T$ saving points, and the convexity loss cannot
exceed the largest spacing, because a budget between two levels is served by the
lower one. Here $m{=}2$ --- tiles with identical rows switch together --- and
the bound is $0.745$ points, which the measured spacing attains exactly. Nothing
in the expression depends on content or rate, and it falls as $1/T$: halving the
tile side puts four times as many tiles on the lattice, each carrying a quarter
of the step. Fine granularity is what makes the Lagrangian relaxation lossless
in practice, not any property of the images.

Two numbers bound what any budget can do (Table~\ref{tab:operating}). The
\textbf{floor} $D_{\min}$ is the distortion of a tiled decode with every tile at
full depth --- pure tiling penalty, \FloorLow$\dB$ at $q0$ rising to
\FloorHigh$\dB$ at $q63$. A budget below it admits no allocation. The
\textbf{saturation} point $D_{\mathrm{sat}}$ is the distortion when every tile
takes exit $j$; any budget at or above it attains $S_{\max}$ and a larger one
attains nothing more.

This has a consequence worth stating plainly: at $q0$ the ceiling is reached at
\SatLow$\dB$. The architectural bound is not an asymptote, it is an operating
point, and beyond it the limiting factor is the \emph{ladder}, not the budget ---
which is an argument for a finer ladder rather than a looser budget. It also
identifies a narrow regime: budgets in
$[\SatLow, \SatWindowHi)\dB$ saturate the lowest rate and nothing else, a window
\SatWindowMb\ millibels wide.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/budget_band.png}
\caption{\textbf{The band is the rate dependence.} \textbf{a} Saving against the
budget, with each rate's floor and saturation point ticked. \textbf{b} The same
with the budget axis rescaled onto each rate's own band. Five curves become one.}
\label{fig:band}
\end{figure}

\textbf{And the window is almost all of the rate dependence.} At a matched
decibel the five rates are \BandRawSpread\ points apart. Rescale the budget axis
onto each rate's own band --- floor at $0$, saturation at $1$ --- and they
collapse onto a single curve, \BandSpreadMean\ points apart on average and
\BandSpreadMax\ at worst (Fig.~\ref{fig:band}). So the answer to ``how much does
a $0.1\dB$ budget buy at this rate'' is, to within a couple of points, ``where
does $0.1\dB$ sit in this rate's band''. The floor and the saturation point are
both in closed form and both cheap to measure; what they leave over is small
enough that a deployment could calibrate the two ends and read the rest off one
curve.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/tradeoff.png}
\caption{\textbf{The trade-off, whole.} \textbf{a} What a budget buys, per rate;
the ceiling is \Ceiling\% and $q0$ reaches it at \SatLow$\dB$. \textbf{b} The
same relation inverted --- what a saving target costs. Both are the curve the
three budgets reported elsewhere are three points of.}
\label{fig:tradeoff}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Signalled versus predicted allocation}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/router_ab.png}
\caption{\textbf{Who decides.} \textbf{(a)} A holds the source, so it can
decode all $K$ exits per tile and pick the true minimiser; it signals the map at
$\sim$\MapBits\ bits/frame. B never sees the source --- a \RouterParams-parameter
head reads $\hat{y}$, the entropy scales and qp --- and signals nothing.
\textbf{(b)} Saving at 0.1\,dB; shading is what a bit-exact bitstream costs.
\textbf{(c)} That cost is smallest at $q\GapMinQp$, where the tilt needed to
move the router off its training multiplier is essentially zero, and grows in
both directions. At $0.3\dB$ it collapses to the router's own
\RouterCostPct\,\% wherever the budget saturates the ladder, and widens where it
does not.}
\label{fig:ab}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/ab}}
\caption{\textbf{Signalled against predicted} at two budgets, same checkpoint and
test set, with one router trained against the deployed oracle at a single
$\lambda$.}
\label{tab:ab}
\end{table}

Configuration~A is exact by construction and costs bits; configuration~B is
approximate and costs none. Table~\ref{tab:ab} is the comparison, and it splits
in two.

\textbf{Not signalling costs \GapMin--\GapMax\ points}, roughly flat across
rate, for zero added bits and a byte-identical file. The gap is smallest at
$q\GapMinQp$ and grows toward both ends.

\textbf{It tracks $|\beta|$}, the tilt the bisection has to apply to move a
router trained at one $\lambda$ onto another operating point. At
$q\BetaMinQp$ the required tilt is $\beta{=}\BetaAtMin$ --- essentially none,
because that is where the training $\lambda$ lands --- and the gap is at its
minimum. At $q0$ the tilt is \BetaLow\ and the gap is \GapMax. A large tilt lets
the cost term dominate the logits and discards the content ranking the router
learned, in either direction. The remedy is not a better architecture but a
router per operating point, which a deployment would have anyway: one set of
weights serves all rates, and a \RouterParams\ head per rate is $0.3\%$ of the
model each.

Loosening the budget closes the gap only where the budget saturates the ladder.
At $0.3\dB$ it is \GapLooseLow\ points at the three lowest rates --- exactly the
router's own \RouterCostPct\% of decode, so its \emph{prediction} is free there:
both configurations send every tile to the cheapest rung and there is nothing
left to predict wrongly. At the two highest rates $0.3\dB$ does not saturate,
and the gap \emph{widens} to \GapLooseHigh\ points, because a looser budget
gives the allocation more room to be wrong in as well as more room to be right.

We report the single-router number because it is the honest one for a system
that trains once, and note that it understates what B can do.

An earlier version of this measurement put the gap at $1.7$ points at $q0$
rising to $13.3$ at $q63$. That was the exit mask: the head suppresses exits
below the split depth by assigning $-10^{4}$, its own logits had drifted to that
scale, and the suppressed entries were therefore the largest in every row ---
so a large share of every tile went to the cheapest rung for a reason unrelated
to its content. The mask is now $-\infty$. Fixing it costs $3.5$ points at $q0$,
where the accident happened to agree with the oracle, and buys $9.4$ at $q63$,
where it did not.

\subsection{A router with no parameters}
\label{sec:raterank}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/raterank.png}
\caption{\textbf{The free baseline.} \textbf{a} Saving at $0.1\dB$; shaded where
the parameter-free rule beats the trained head. \textbf{b} What a tile's bit
count is correlated with, against how often the rule agrees with the oracle
outright; dotted is the head's own held-out agreement.}
\label{fig:raterank}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/raterank}}
\caption{\textbf{The free baseline}, $0.1\dB$, same test set. Bold where the
parameter-free rule beats the trained head. $\rho$ are Spearman correlations
between a tile's bit count and, respectively, the depth the oracle assigns it and
the distortion it stands to gain from that depth.}
\label{tab:raterank}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/blend}}
\caption{\textbf{Blending the two decoder-side signals} at $0.1\dB$, both
normalised to unit mean, weight $w$ from the bit rule to the head's ordering.
Bold is the best per rate.}
\label{tab:blend}
\end{table}

Before a $\RouterParams$ head is worth its \RouterCostPct\% of the decode, it has
to beat what the decoder already knows. The entropy model has produced a number
per tile before the trunk runs and at no cost: how many bits that tile's latents
took.

We turn it into a routing rule with no learned parameters. Model the per-tile
distortion as rank-1 in the log domain,
$\log D(t,k)\approx\alpha\log b(t)+c+\log\varphi_k$, where $b$ is the tile's bit
count normalised by the frame mean and $\varphi$ is a $K$-vector saying what each
exit costs on an average tile. Fit $(\alpha,c,\varphi)$ by least squares,
leave-one-sequence-out so no sequence contributes to the profile that routes it,
and run the same Lagrangian the oracle runs on the surrogate. Nothing is
signalled, nothing is trained, and the arithmetic is a scalar per tile.

\textbf{It matches the trained head to within a point either way.} It beats the
\RouterParams\ router at the \RateRankNWins\ lowest rates, by up to
\RateRankBeatsBy\ points, and loses at the two highest by at most
\RateRankLosesBy. That is the whole margin between a parameter-free rule and a
head that was trained on this decoder against this oracle, and the free rule
carries none of the head's \RouterCostPct\% of decode.

\textbf{Why it works is not that it agrees with the oracle.} It agrees on
\RateRankAgreeLo--\RateRankAgreeHi\ of tiles, well below the router's $0.718$,
and still saves more at three of five rates. Agreement counts a disagreement on
a tile where two exits are within a hair of each other exactly as heavily as one
where the choice is most of the frame's error, and most tiles are the former.
What the rule gets right is the ordering that matters: bits correlate with the
\emph{spread} across the ladder --- how much a tile stands to gain from depth ---
at $\rho_{\mathrm{spread}}=\RateRankSpreadLo$--\RateRankSpreadHi\ at every rate.

\textbf{At a looser budget it stops being a baseline and becomes the answer.}
At $0.3\dB$ it reaches the architectural ceiling exactly at the
\RateRankLooseCeil\ lowest rates, is within $0.2$ points of the oracle at $q48$,
and gives up \RateRankLoose\% against the oracle's \SigLooseHigh\% at $q63$ ---
better than the trained head at every rate, by up to \RateRankLooseAheadBy\
points --- the head is charged for itself and this is not, and at a loose budget
its ordering has less left to contribute. Once the budget saturates the ladder there is little
ordering left to get right, and the free rule gets it.

\textbf{What it cannot do} is see anything beyond that ordering. A rank-1 model
in the level assigns every tile the same relative profile over exits, so $b$ only
decides where on the ladder a tile falls, never the shape of its trade-off. That
is the ceiling this baseline sits at, and it is the part a learned head should be
earning its parameters on. Ours does, at low rate, and does not at high rate.

Per-block bit allocation is a standard quantity in learned compression, where it
is something to \emph{choose}: block-level rate control sets it so that complex
regions get more bits~\cite{blockratecontrol}. We read the same number in the
other direction, after the fact and at the decoder, as a statement about how hard
a region was --- which costs nothing precisely because someone else already paid
for it.

\textbf{Are the two signals complementary?} Barely. Normalising both surrogates
to unit mean and blending them with one weight $w$ --- $w{=}0$ the bit rule,
$w{=}1$ the head's ordering --- the best blend is $w{=}0$ at the three lowest
rates and a small head weight at the two highest, worth $+2.1$ points at $q48$
and $+0.9$ at $q63$ (Table~\ref{tab:blend}). The head reads the entropy model's
scales, so it already has most of what the bit count carries; what it adds is
confined to the regime where the free rule was losing anyway.

We report this because a learned component should be measured against the free
alternative and rarely is. In adaptive inference the usual controls are a uniform
allocation and a random one; both are far weaker than a decoder-side signal that
happens to be lying around.

\subsection{Signalling only what the router gets wrong}
\label{sec:hybrid}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/hybrid.png}
\caption{\textbf{Partial signalling.} \textbf{a} Saving against the bits spent
on the map; the left end of each line is B and the right end is A.
\textbf{b} The same, normalised: what fraction of the A--B gap a given fraction
of the map recovers; dashed is proportional recovery, and above $100\%$ a
partial map is beating a complete one. \textbf{c} The same against the
fixed-$\lambda$ Lorenz prediction; dashed is equality, and points above it are
allocations a single multiplier cannot reach.}
\label{fig:hybrid}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/hybrid}}
\caption{\textbf{Configuration C} at $0.1\dB$. Columns are the fraction of tiles
the encoder overrides; the two end columns reproduce B and A to within
$0.1$ points, which is the check that the interpolation is real.}
\label{tab:hybrid}
\end{table}

A and B are the two ends of a single scale, not two designs. The encoder can
run the decoder's router --- it reads only decoded data --- so it knows, tile by
tile, where the prediction will be wrong. Nothing forces it to correct all of
them.

Configuration C signals a fraction $\rho$ of the tiles and leaves the rest to
the router. The overrides are chosen by Lagrangian regret,
$\Delta(t)=L_\lambda(t,\hat{k})-L_\lambda(t,k^{*})$, which is exactly what the
objective loses on that tile by staying silent; $\beta$ is held at B's value and
$\lambda$ is bisected over the overrides to land back on the budget. The map
costs an entropy-coded mask, $N H_2(\rho)$ bits, plus $3$ per override.

\textbf{The two ends check out.} At $\rho{=}0$ the measurement reproduces
configuration~B to the second decimal at every rate, and at $\rho{=}1$ it
reproduces~A. Neither is imposed --- both fall out of the same code path against
independently measured files --- so the columns between them measure something
real.

\textbf{Most of the gap is cheap.} Overriding a tenth of the tiles for
\HybridBitsTenth\ bits per frame recovers
\HybridRecoverTenthLow--\HybridRecoverTenthHigh\% of the gap and a fifth
recovers \HybridRecoverFifthLow--\HybridRecoverFifthHigh\%. Recovery is concave
everywhere, so the first bits spent are the most useful ones.

\textbf{And a partial map can beat a complete one.} At \HybridBeatsAN\ of
\HybridBeatsAOf\ rates, signalling half the tiles for \HybridBitsHalf\ bits
saves \emph{more} than signalling all of them --- up to \HybridBeatsABy\ points
--- at the same distortion. Both land within the bisection's $5\times10^{-4}\dB$
tolerance of the budget, and the local exchange rate is about $48$ saving points
per decibel, so the tolerance is worth $0.02$ points against a margin ten to
twenty times that. It is not noise, and it is not a better predictor:
the hybrid has \emph{two} multipliers where A has one. The oracle's $\lambda$
governs the overridden tiles and the router's fixed $\beta$ the rest, and a
two-multiplier allocation reaches points on the distortion--compute plane that a
single Lagrangian sweep cannot, for the same reason the sweep misses interior
Pareto points at all (Section~\ref{sec:operating}). Configuration~A is optimal
among allocations reachable by one multiplier, which is a smaller set than it
sounds.

\textbf{Why the recovery is concave, and what bounds it.} At a fixed $\lambda$
the objective is separable, so overriding a set removes \emph{exactly} the sum
of that set's regrets: the recovery of the \emph{objective} is the Lorenz curve
of the per-tile regret distribution, and its curvature is that distribution's
Gini coefficient, \GiniMin--\GiniMax\ across rates. What the table reports is
not objective but saving at fixed distortion, and returning to the budget means
re-bisecting $\lambda$ --- which is also what lets the two-multiplier
allocations above escape the bound.

\textbf{At the loose budget it matters where the gap is.} At $0.3\dB$ the three
lowest rates are saturated and there is nothing for a partial map to buy. At
\HybridLooseQps, where the gap is \GapLooseHigh\ points, half the map recovers
\HybridLooseRecLo--\HybridLooseRecHi\% of it. The rule is the same one the
allocation follows everywhere: spend the bits where the ladder still has
somewhere to go.

\textbf{Which predictor should C be built on?} Either --- and the answer follows
the same split as Section~\ref{sec:raterank}. Running the identical override
rule over the parameter-free surrogate instead of the head is worth up to
\CPredBitsAhead\ points at the lowest rate and costs up to \CPredHeadAhead\ at
the highest. Both converge on A at $\rho{=}1$ to the second decimal at every
rate, which is the third independent check that the two code paths agree. The
best single operating point we measured is the free predictor with half the map
signalled: \CBestSave\% at $q\CBestQp$, \CBestOverA\ points \emph{above} full
signalling, with no learned component anywhere in the decoder.

Configuration C is what we would ship where a small map is tolerable and a large
one is not. It also reframes the A--B gap: it is not the price of prediction,
it is the price of \emph{silence}, and silence is priced per tile.

\subsection{Does the map have to be recomputed?}
\label{sec:transfer}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/map_transfer.png}
\caption{\textbf{Reusing an exit map.} Solid is the transferred map, dashed the
one recomputed in place. \textbf{a}, \textbf{b}: reuse across frames of the same
sequence. \textbf{c}: reuse across quality index; the entry is the delivered
distortion against a $0.1\dB$ budget.}
\label{fig:transfer}
\end{figure}

Configuration A costs the encoder about one extra decode per frame. Whether that
matters depends on how often the map has to be recomputed, which nobody has
checked.

\textbf{Across time it barely has to be.} Taking frame 0's map and applying it
eight frames later costs \TransferDbCost$\dB$ at $q0$ --- five percent of the
budget --- and
no saving at all: \TransferSaving\% transferred against
\TransferInPlaceLo--\TransferInPlaceHi\% recomputed. The
allocation is a property of where the content is hard, and that moves slowly. A
codec would search once per group of pictures rather than once per frame, and
divide the encoder cost by the group length.

\textbf{Across rate it very much does}, and the direction matters. The map found
at $q0$ applied at $q63$ delivers \TransferCrossDb$\dB$ against a $0.1\dB$
budget: it claims
the low-rate saving of \TransferSaving\% while spending nearly twice the
quality it is
allowed. The reverse is safe but wasteful --- the $q63$ map applied at $q0$
delivers $0.075\dB$ and only $19.8\%$ where $33.1\%$ was available. Shallow exits
are cheap in quality at low rate and expensive at high rate, so a map is
calibrated to the rate it was found at and reusing it upward silently breaks the
quality guarantee.

The practical reading: search once per rate, reuse across frames.

\subsection{Complexity and wall-clock}
\label{sec:wallclock}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/complexity}
\caption{\textbf{Decoder complexity} at 1080p. Our deepest exit costs slightly
more than the release because it still pays the seam-repair module; that
$1.0095$, not $1.0$, is what every saving in this paper is \emph{not} divided by.
Wall-clock is the sorted loop of Section~\ref{sec:wallclock}.}
\label{tab:complexity}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/latency}
\caption{\textbf{Wall-clock}, 1080p, median of 40 interleaved iterations on one
A100-class GPU, at the $0.1\dB$ operating point. ``MACs'' is what the arithmetic
predicts; ``measured'' is the sorted per-tile loop of
Section~\ref{sec:wallclock}.}
\label{tab:latency}
\end{table}

A saving in multiply--accumulates is not a saving in time. Tiling itself costs
\TilingOverhead\% before anything exits early --- the deepest-exit tiled decode
against the released full-frame one, same arithmetic, same weights --- and the
routed decode realises \WallMasked\% at $q0$ against the \WallPredicted\% its
operations predict. Four fifths of the predicted saving arrives; the missing
fifth is the tiling overhead plus the bookkeeping of a shrinking active set,
which a MAC count cannot see. The shortfall is proportional rather than
constant: \WallHighMeasured\% realised against \WallHighPredicted\% at $q63$.

Sorting the tiles once by exit depth recovers part of it. The obvious
implementation of a shrinking active set --- a boolean mask, a gather of
survivors and a scatter of the finished, at every group boundary --- forces a
device-to-host synchronisation per boundary. Descending by exit depth, ``still
active at group $g$'' becomes a contiguous prefix instead: each group is a slice
rather than a gather, the boundaries come from one cumulative count rather than
a mask per group, and the finished tiles return through the inverse permutation
in a single scatter. The arithmetic is unchanged and the output is bit-identical
on GPU. The saving at $q0$ goes from \WallMasked\% to \WallSorted\%
(Table~\ref{tab:latency}) --- \WallSortedGain\ points, a fifth of the shortfall,
for a change that touches no arithmetic.

The same lesson applies to our own accounting. Every configuration~B number in
this paper charges the router at its share of the decoder's
multiply--accumulates, \RouterCostPct\%. Timed on the padded $2048{\times}1280$
frame the decoder actually sees, interleaved against a deepest-exit decode so a
co-tenant's load lands on both equally, the head costs \RouterTimePct\% ---
\RouterTimeFactor$\times$ what its arithmetic predicts, and for the same reason
as everything else in this section: a \RouterParams-parameter head is launch
overhead, and a MAC count cannot see a launch. Charged at measured time rather
than at operations, every B number in this paper would fall by a further
\RouterTimeExtra\ points. We leave them charged at MACs because that is the
convention the rest of the literature reports in, and record the correction
here rather than letting it sit unstated.

We report the shortfall because a paper that quotes only operations would
report \WallPredicted\% where the same code, run as written, delivers
\WallSorted\%. The direction is the one that matters: operations are an
\emph{optimistic} bound on this method, and the optimism grows with how much of
the frame exits early.

\subsection{The right ladder depends on the budget}
\label{sec:ladder}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/runs}}
\caption{\textbf{Ladder configurations}, mean saving (\%) over the five rates,
same test set and protocol. ``Ceiling'' is Eq.~(\ref{eq:ceiling}).
$^{\ast}$ one rate is infeasible at that budget --- the ladder's floor exceeds
it --- so the mean is over the remaining four.}
\label{tab:runs}
\end{table}

Section~\ref{sec:operating} argued that once a budget saturates a ladder the
only way to spend more is a rung that does not exist. Table~\ref{tab:runs}
measures it. A finer ladder ($K{=}12$, $j{=}4$) has a ceiling of $50.3\%$
against \Ceiling\%, and the two orderings cross between $0.1$ and $0.3\dB$:

\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
\item At $0.1\dB$ the coarse ladder wins, and the fine one cannot even reach the
      budget at the highest rate. Splitting later ($j{=}4$ against $j{=}2$) puts
      twice as many blocks in the per-tile section, which by
      Eq.~(\ref{eq:contam}) raises the floor.
\item At $0.5\dB$ the fine ladder wins by $6.7$ points, \FineHalfDb\% against
      \CoarseHalfDb\%, because the coarse one has been pinned at its ceiling
      since $0.3\dB$ and has nothing left to give.
\end{itemize}

So the ladder is not a hyperparameter to be tuned once. It is a function of the
operating point, and the floor--saturation window of
Section~\ref{sec:operating} is what tells you which side of the crossover you are
on.

% =========================================================== limitations
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}

\paragraph{The seam is reduced, and the exact remedy is not usable as it stands.}
Section~\ref{sec:coupling} shows that canvas coupling removes
\CoupFloorDropLo--\CoupFloorDropHi\% of the
floor and is bit-exact at uniform depth, yet collapses the routed saving because
routing puts neighbouring tiles at different depths. Whether a decoder trained
with coupling recovers both at once is open, and it is the experiment we would
run next. Until it exists, the floor is a cost this method pays.

\paragraph{Intra frames only.} This is the image path of a video codec. Extending
the ladder to inter frames raises a question this paper does not answer: an exit
map propagates through the reference chain, so a shallow tile in one frame is a
worse reference for the next.

\paragraph{Training is not converged.} The measured saving is still increasing at
every checkpoint we have measured more than once, so the numbers here are a lower
bound rather than a converged result.

\paragraph{A single decoder.} All results are on DCVC-UF's intra decoder.
Nothing in the method is specific to it --- the ladder needs only a residual
trunk with a shared head --- but that is an argument, not a measurement.

% =========================================================== conclusion
\section{Conclusion}

Learned decoders spend a constant amount of computation on a non-constant world.
An early-exit ladder over the tiles of a frame recovers a substantial fraction of
it --- \MainLowRate\% to \MainHighRate\% of decoder MACs for a $0.1\dB$ budget,
at a BD-Rate cost of \BdRateALow\% --- without touching the encoder or the coded
payload.

Three lessons we would carry to any spatially adaptive decoder, none of them
about early exit.

\textbf{Tiling is the dominant cost and it is governed by depth.} Its entire
cause is a single $3\times3$ that is $0.29\%$ of the arithmetic; the penalty
grows as the square of how many such convolutions run per tile; and the
corrupted-area fraction usually quoted predicts it badly.

\textbf{The exact remedy is in tension with the thing it enables.} Giving each
convolution its real neighbour is bit-identical at uniform depth and collapses
the allocation under routing, because routing is the deliberate violation of the
condition that makes it exact. Any method combining spatial adaptivity with tiled
inference will walk into this.

\textbf{A quality budget is only a control variable inside a measurable window.}
Below the floor it admits nothing, above saturation it buys nothing, and
reporting a saving without saying where in that window it sits leaves out the
most useful part of the result.

And three cautions about measuring any of it. A saving in operations is an
optimistic bound on a saving in time, and the optimism scales with the saving.
A learned router should be compared against a free one: routing on the bits
already spent per tile needs no parameters, no training and no bits, and it beats
our trained head to within \RateRankLosesBy\ points at every rate --- while
agreeing with the oracle on fewer tiles than the head does, which is a warning
about the metric as much as about the head. And a timing
harness will report numbers whether or not it is timing the right device ---
this one did, for months, and the tell was a decoder that appeared to slow down
with the quality index.
